Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM6238 : BioMEMS and Biosensors { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I: Introduction to MEMS and BioMEMS
• Overview of MEMS and BioMEMS: Definitions, historical background, and significance.
• Silicon Microfabrication: Materials, fabrication methods, and techniques.
• Soft Substrate Microfabrication: Materials and fabrication methods specific to soft substrates.
• Biomedical Applications of MEMS Devices: Key applications and examples.
• Emerging Devices and Applications: New developments and innovative uses.
• Limitations of MEMS and BioMEMS: Challenges in design, fabrication, and application.
Module 2 :

Module II: Fundamentals of MEMS
• Principles and Fabrication Technologies: Introduction to core MEMS principles and methods.
• MEMS Structures and Materials: Overview of basic structures and materials used in MEMS.
• Design, Fabrication, and Packaging: Key considerations in the MEMS development process.
• Characteristics of Microstructures:
Mechanical properties
Electrical characteristics
Optical attributes
Biochemical and fluidic properties
Module 3 :

Module III: Microfabrication Techniques
• Concepts and Types of Microfabrication:
Thin Film Deposition
Lithography Methods: Photolithography, E-Beam Lithography, X-ray Lithography, Soft Lithography
Etching: Dry and wet etching techniques
Wafer Bonding
Bulk and Surface Micromachining
LIGA Process (Lithography, Electroplating, and Molding)
• Examples of MEMS and BioMEMS Devices: Practical applications and case studies.
• Introduction to Biosensors:
Basic Elements and Design
Fabrication Techniques and Materials
Types and Principles of Biosensors
• Lab-on-a-Chip (LoC):
Components: Microsensors, lenses, heaters, and actuators.
Minimally invasive biomedical devices.
Future prospects of LoC technology.
Module 4 :

Module IV: BioMEMS for Clinical Detection
• Micro and Nano Fabrication for Biochips and LoC:
Fundamentals and techniques.
Principles of molecular recognition and bio-immobilization.
• On-Chip Biochemical Detection:
Methods and technologies.
• Introduction to Micro/Nanofluidics:
Basic concepts and applications.
• Integration of Lab-on-a-Chip Components: Sensors, microfluidic channels, and other system elements.
Module 5 :

Module V: Biosensors and Biochips
• Fundamentals of Biosensors:
Basics of electrochemistry and electrochemical biosensors.
• Microfluidic Devices and Systems: Role in biomedical applications.
• MEMS Sensors and Actuators: Medical instrumentation uses.
• Bioelectronics:
Fundamentals of biosignal conditioning and processing.
• Biosensors for Health:
Applications in diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, and cancer detection.
• MOSFET Biosensors:
Basic principles and examples of use.
• Ion Exchange Membrane Electrodes and Enzyme Electrodes: Applications in diagnostics.

Course Objective

1 .


To aware the students about the fundamental principles of microsystems (MEMS and BioMEMS).

2 .

To provide the concepts essential for designing lab-on-a-chip and Point-of-care devices for biomedical applications.

3 .

To provide the concept of Biosensors, uses, design, and development for advanced research level so that students would be comfortable in higher studies.

4 .

To Hands-on experience in in-house microfabrication (Photolithography) and Hands-on experience in fabricating simple LoC devices.

Course Outcome

1 .

After completing the course, the students will be able to:
know the various MEMS design and fabrication techniques for Biosensors. Explore the concepts of BioMEMS & its application in healthcare.

2 .


Ability to identify basic requirements for a design application related to microfabrication and its techniques for biomedical systems.

3 .


To develop the skill to realize, build, and get hands-on experience fabricating simple LoC devices.

4 .


To analyze, compare, and appreciate the performance and merit of different lab-on-a-chip concepts, designs, and modes of work.
5 .

To know the different biosensors for biomedical applications, analyze, compare, and appreciate the performance and merit of different and point-of-care devices' concepts, importance, design, and work mode.

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : LS3008 : Infection and Immunity { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I: Introduction to Infection and Immunity: Overview of infectious diseases: bacterial, viral, fungal, and parasitic infections. Host-pathogen interactions: principles and co-evolution. Basics of immune recognition and activation against pathogens.
Module II: Host Defense Mechanisms Against Pathogens: Bacterial infections: phagocytosis, complement activation, and antibody-mediated responses Viral infections: interferons, NK cells, and cytotoxic T-cell responses Fungal and parasitic infections: macrophage activity and T-helper cell roles, Immune memory and long-term protection against reinfection.
Module III: Pathogen Strategies for Immune Evasion: Mechanisms of immune evasion: antigenic variation, inhibition of immune signalling, and biofilm formation, Case studies: HIV, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Plasmodium spp. , Implications of immune evasion on disease progression and therapeutic strategies.
Module IV: Vaccines and Immunotherapies: Vaccine types: live-attenuated, inactivated, subunit, mRNA, and DNA vaccines, Role of adjuvants in enhancing immune responses, Immunotherapy approaches: monoclonal antibodies, checkpoint inhibitors, and CAR-T cells, Challenges in vaccine development and deployment for emerging diseases.
Module V: Emerging Infectious Diseases and Global Challenges: Emerging and re-emerging infections: zoonotic diseases and pandemic threats, Case studies: SARS-CoV-2, Zika virus, and antimicrobial-resistant bacteria, Ethical and social considerations in vaccine distribution and global health policy.

Course Objective

1 .

To introduce the biological mechanisms underlying infectious diseases and immune responses.
2 .

To study microbial immune evasion strategies and their impact on infection progression.
3 .

To explore the principles and applications of vaccines and immunotherapies in disease prevention and treatment.

Course Outcome

1 .

By the end of the course, students will be able to:
1. Explain host-pathogen dynamics and immune defence mechanisms.
2. Evaluate the scientific principles behind vaccines and immunotherapies.
3. Apply knowledge to understand emerging infectious diseases and global health challenges.

7059.t: ME3303: Fluid Dynamics and Hydraulic Machines
7059.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : ME3303 : Fluid Dynamics and Hydraulic Machines { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Dimensional analysis and similarity
Contact hours = 6
Introduction; dimensions; MLT-theta and FLT-theta systems; the principle of dimensional homogeneity; dimensions of some common fluid mechanics properties; non dimensional parameters of some common fluid mechanics processes; the pi theorem; nondimensionalization of the basic equations; continuity; momentum; boundary conditions; modelling and similarity; model and prototype; geometric similarity; kinematic similarity; dynamic similarity
Module 2 :

Boundary layer theory
Contact hours = 6
Introduction; boundary layer thickness; skin friction coefficient; pressure coefficient; drag and lift coefficients; Prandtl’s boundary layer approximations; introduction to laminar and turbulent boundary layers; momentum integral estimates; displacement thickness; momentum thickness; von Karman momentum integral analysis for laminar and turbulent boundary layers on flat plates; flat plate boundary layer equations; Blasius similarity solution; qualitative description on the boundary layers with pressure gradient and boundary layer separation
Module 3 :

Compressible flow
Contact hours = 6
Introduction and review of thermodynamics; the Mach number; the specific heat ratio; the perfect gas approximation; isentropic process; the speed of sound; adiabatic and isentropic steady flow; Mach number relations; stagnation properties; critical values at sonic point; isentropic flow with area changes; the normal shock wave; Rankine–Hugoniot relations; Mach number relations; operation of converging and converging-diverging nozzles
Module 4 :

Hydraulic machines
Contact hours = 12
Introduction and classification; positive displacement pumps; dynamic pumps; the centrifugal pump; energy balance and basic parameters; flow rate; head; power; efficiency; elementary pump theory; effect of blade angle on pump head; deviation from ideal pump theory; net positive suction head; dimensionless pump parameters; pump performance curves and similarity rules; best efficiency point; the specific speed; mixed- and axial-flow pumps; matching pumps to system characteristics; turbines; impulse and reaction turbines; idealized theory for reaction turbines; power specific speed; qualitative description on hydroelectric power plants; draft tube; impulse turbines; idealized theory for Pelton turbines; best efficiency condition
Module 5 :

Potential flow
Contact hours = 6
Introduction; review of velocity potential concepts; review of stream function concepts; potential flow equations; elementary plane flow solutions; uniform stream; line source or sink at the origin; line irrotational vortex; superposition of plane flow solutions; source plus and equal sink; the doublet; sink plus vortex at the origin; the Rankine half body; circulation; plane flow past closed-body shapes; the Ranking oval; flow past a circular cylinder with and without circulation; D’Alembert’s paradox; Kutta-Joukowaski lift theorem

Course Objective

1 .

To understand and apply the dimensional analysis and similarity principles for planning and/or analyzing a flow process
2 .

To understand the basic concepts of boundary layer theory, and apply the same for drag, lift and boundary flow analysis
3 .

To recognize different aspects of compressible flow processes, and to perform some elementary analysis of the same
4 .

To understand the working principles of hydraulic machines, and to evaluate the planning and selection of hydraulic machine systems
5 .

To understand the principles of potential flow, and to apply the same to construct complex flow structures of practical relevance

Course Outcome

1 .

To understand and apply the dimensional analysis and similarity principles for planning and/or analyzing a flow process
2 .

To understand the basic concepts of boundary layer theory, and apply the same for drag, lift and boundary flow analysis

To recognize different aspects of compressible flow processes, and to perform some elementary analysis of the same
4 .

To understand the working principles of hydraulic machines, and to evaluate the planning and selection of hydraulic machine systems
5 .

To understand the principles of potential flow, and to apply the same to construct complex flow structures of practical relevance

Subject {L-T-P / C} : PH5102 : Biophysics { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

(8 hrs) Biomolecular interactions and dynamics. Introduction to Biophysics, spatial and temporal scales. steric, van der Waals, Coulomb and hydrophobic interactions, protein structure and folding, molecular dynamics, Brownian dynamics

Module 2 :

(6 hrs) Diffusion. Life at low Reynol’ds number, random walks and diffusion, methods to measure the diffusion coefficient: single particle tracking, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), fluorescence correlation spectroscopy, diffusion and cell signaling

Module 3 :

(8 hrs) Polymers. Introduction, freely jointed chain, freely rotating chain, Gaussian chain, Universality and Self-similarity, Scaling analysis

Module 4 :

(4 hrs) Understanding Chemical Kinetics for two-state system, From kinetics to thermodynamics, Michelis-Menten reaction

Module 5 :

(6 hrs) Equilibrium thermodynamics and statistical Mechanics. Laws of thermodynamics and entropy principle, microcanonical, canonical, grand canonical ensemble, ideal gas, phase transitions

Module 6 :

(3 hours) Fluid flows in biology, viscosity and Navier Stokes equation

Course Objective

1 .

To have a basic understanding of the protein structural hierarchy and forces governing biomolecular assembly and dynamics
2 .

To learn about diffusion in dilute and cellular environments
3 .

To understand the physical properties of long peptide chains
4 .

To understand the kinetics of biomolecular reactions
5 .

To understand why biological systems are marginally stable due to enthalpy-entropy balance
6 .

To learn about flow of fluids in biological systems

Course Outcome

1 .

At the end of course, students will be able to:
CO1: Explain how various forces stabilize biomolecular structures
2 .

CO2: Explain how cellular environment can influence diffusion of a tracer particle
3 .

CO3: Explain structural and dynamical characteristics of long peptide chains

4 .

CO4: Calculate biomolecular reaction rates and free energy changes
5 .

CO5: Analyze experimental and theoretical investigation biomolecular events
